thread.title: Apple to appeal court decision to revive lawsuit over iPhone app charges

title: Apple to appeal court decision to revive lawsuit over iPhone app charges
text:
Download PDF version 07:26 26 Nov 2018 Apple has been accused of violating federal antitrust laws by requiring apps to be sold through the App Store and then taking a 30% commission from the purchases A group of iPhone users claim Apple’s monopoly on mobile apps leads to inflated prices
The US Supreme Court will on Monday hear Apple Inc’s (LON:AAPL) appeal against a lower court’s decision to revive a class-action lawsuit accusing the company of forcing consumers to overpay for iPhone apps.
The lawsuit, filed by a group of iPhone users in a California federal court in 2011, claims the tech giant violated federal antitrust laws by requiring apps to be sold through the firm’s App Store and then taking a 30% commission from the purchases. READ: Apple shares tank as supplier warnings fuel concerns about iPhone sales
Developers set the prices of their apps but Apple collects the payments from the iPhone users and keeps the commission paid on each purchase.
The iPhone users, including lead plaintiff Robert Pepper of Chicago, said Apple’s monopoly on mobile apps leads to inflated prices.
The parties involved the case argued over whether app developers pass on the cost of the commission to consumers.
Apple said developers earned more than US$26bn in 2017, up 30% on the previous year.
The company told justices in legal papers that ruling in favour of the iPhone users would hurt the e-commerce sector, which generates hundreds of billions of dollars in US retail sales each year.
The plaintiffs said app developers would be unlikely to sue Apple since the company controls the service they make money from, meaning there was no one to challenge the alleged anti-competitive behaviour.
Apple argued that the plaintiffs lacked the required legal standing to bring the lawsuit.
A federal judge in Oakland, California sided with Apple, saying the consumers were not direct purchasers because the higher fees they paid were passed on by the developers.
However, the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals revived the case last year, ruling that Apple was a distributor that sold iPhone apps directly to consumers. Top stories
